name: Sarangapani Temple, Kumbakonam
deity: Vishnu as Sarangapani, bearer of the bow Sarnga, reclining as Aravamudan
period: Chola origins; the towering gateway raised under later Nayaka rule
summary: In the temple-town of Kumbakonam, Vishnu descends from Vaikuntha in a stone chariot: the sanctum of Sarangapani is carved as a great ratha drawn by horses and elephants, entered beneath one of the tallest temple gateways in the south — a Divya Desam ranked among the foremost abodes of Vishnu.

sections.history: The Sarangapani temple is the greatest Vishnu shrine of Kumbakonam, the ancient Chola temple-town on the Kaveri once called Kudanthai. It is a Divya Desam sung by the Alvars as Thirukudanthai, and tradition sets it among the highest Vaishnava temples of the south, in the company of Srirangam and Tirumala. The temple grew from Chola foundations, and its soaring main gateway was raised in the later centuries under Nayaka patronage. Kumbakonam itself is a dense knot of temples on the river, and Sarangapani stands at its Vaishnava heart, its worship carried by an unbroken Sri Vaishnava tradition and the hymns of the Alvar poet-saints.
sections.architecture: The sanctum is the temple's marvel: it is shaped as a vast chariot, a ratha, complete with great stone wheels and drawn by carved horses and elephants, so that the shrine itself becomes the celestial vehicle in which Vishnu is said to have descended to earth. Within it the lord reclines as Aravamudan, 'the insatiable nectar'. The complex is entered from the south beneath an immense eleven-tiered rajagopuram, among the tallest in the Tamil country, and it has two ceremonial gateways — a northern and a southern — used in the two halves of the solar year, marking the sun's northward and southward courses. The golden-lotus tank, the Potramarai, lies within, and pillared halls and sculptured mandapas fill the enclosures in the mature Dravidian manner.
sections.legends: The temple's legend tells of the sage Hema Rishi, who did penance on the bank of the golden-lotus tank longing for the Goddess as his daughter. Lakshmi rose from the tank as Komalavalli, and Vishnu came down from Vaikuntha in his chariot to Kumbakonam to wed her — the very descent that the chariot-shaped sanctum commemorates. As Sarangapani he bears the Sarnga, the divine bow, and as Aravamudan he is the nectar of which the devotee can never have enough, a name given by the Alvar Nammalvar in his rapture before the reclining lord. The two gateways and the sun's turning are woven into the same story of the god who comes to earth to answer love.
sections.festivals: The great festival is the Brahmotsavam in the Tamil spring, when Sarangapani is drawn through Kumbakonam on towering temple cars; the chariot festival is among the most spectacular of the delta. Vaikunta Ekadasi, the float festival on the Potramarai tank, and the observances of the Sri Vaishnava calendar mark the year. Kumbakonam's town-wide Mahamaham, held once in twelve years when many rivers are believed to meet in its great tank, fills every shrine of the town, Sarangapani among them, with vast crowds of pilgrims.
sections.experience: Sarangapani is the heart of a temple-town made for unhurried pilgrimage: Kumbakonam packs many great shrines within a short walk, and the delta around it holds the Chola masterpieces of Darasuram and Gangaikonda Cholapuram and, a little further, island Srirangam. Standing before the chariot-sanctum, with its stone wheels and straining horses, one feels the temple as a vehicle in motion rather than a building at rest. The town is reached easily by road and rail from Thanjavur and Tiruchirapalli, at the green centre of the Kaveri country.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a long midday closure; festival days are busiest. Confirm current timings before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. As a living temple, respectful conduct is asked of all visitors.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted, especially in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Kumbakonam is in Tamil Nadu's Thanjavur district, well connected by road and rail; it lies about 40 km from Thanjavur and Tiruchirapalli, at the centre of the Kaveri delta's temple country.
